title: Software fundamentals matter more than ever: why specs-to-code fails and how old books fix AI coding
summary: Matt Pocock argues that "specs-to-code" produces ever-worse code because it divests from design, and that classic books (Ousterhout, Pragmatic Programmer, Brooks, DDD, Beck) give the fixes. He walks through AI coding failure modes with a skill for each: grilling for shared understanding, a ubiquitous language, TDD, deep modules, and delegating implementation behind designed interfaces.

principles.text: Bad code is more expensive than ever; code is not cheap, because a hard-to-change codebase blocks what AI can offer.
principles.quote: I think code is not cheap. In fact, bad code is the most expensive it's ever been.

principles.text: Specs-to-code fails: repeatedly recompiling specs without looking at the code just yields software entropy and garbage.
principles.quote: The idea that we can just ignore the code and just have the code let it manage itself is just sort of vibe coding by another name.

principles.text: Reach a shared design concept with the AI before building by having it grill you relentlessly, rather than rushing to a plan.
principles.quote: Interview me relentlessly about every aspect of this plan until we reach a shared understanding.

principles.text: Create a ubiquitous language with the AI; shared terms make its thinking less verbose and implementation more aligned.
principles.quote: It's essentially a markdown file full of a list of terms that you and the AI have in common.

principles.text: Feedback rate is your speed limit; use static types, browser access and tests, and use TDD to force small steps.
principles.quote: The rate of feedback is your speed limit, which means that you should be testing as you go, taking small deliberate steps.

principles.text: Structure code as deep modules with simple interfaces; they are easier for AI to navigate and for you to test.
principles.quote: They should be relatively few large deep modules with simple interfaces.
